statement: What are Some Variations of Heathenism? Other terms used to describe variations of, or traditions similar to Heathenism, are Asatru, Vanatru, Odinism, Theodism, Norse-Paganism, and various other more obscure traditions. Odinism tends to focus more so on Odin as the leader or head of the gods/goddesses.

statement: Reach up with your wand or fingers and draw this ball of energy with your wand and touch your forehead and loudly call out in a galdr (chanting) tone: “ASGARD!” Briefly now touch your heart area and then point your wand or fingers down towards the floor and loudly call out in galdr: “MIDGARD!” Now touch your right shoulder: “MUSPELHEIM!” Touch your left shoulder: “NIFLHEIM!” Now bring both hands together like a prayer pose at your heart, the wand can be between the hands: “ALFHEIM” Make a Hammer Sign to the east: “Thor Hallow!” Make a Hammer sign to the south: “Thor Hallow!” Now make a Hammer sign to the west: “Thor Hallow!” Make a Hammer sign to the north: “Thor Hallow!” Face again east and extend both hands outward and hold them this was for the next parts.: In a chanting voice: “Hail Odin who is before me.” “Hail Freyja who is behind me.

statement: I found these at another site and like them a great deal.: > Beauty > The pursuit of beauty and elegance in thought, form and speech. > > Courage/Passion > Zeal, vigor; the strength and courage that comes from a life worth living. > > Land-rightness > The recognition of nature and the environment as worthy of respect, care and reverence. > > Even-mood > Harmonious and balanced thought and action; tranquility, calm, serenity. > > Openness > The quality of being receptive to the world around one, non-judgmental and open. > > Wildness/Ecstasy > Music and dance; the nurturing of inner wildness and childlike being, being like the “fey” > > Love > The all-encompassing force; love for family, for kin, for humanity, for all beings. > > Frith > The peace and goodwill between people bound together; loyalty and the keeping of one’s word. > > Faith/Piety > The trust that the Gods exist and are worthy of our worship, and Their ways worth following. > > Giving > The binding of two parties into one common bond, generosity and hospitality. > > Joy > Wonder and innocence, the recognition that life is worth living, and worth living well. > > Brotherhood > The recognition that we – humans, animals, plants, spirits – are all part of the grander scheme of life, and we share a common heritage, as children of the Earth.

Bless me, my Lady Freyja, that I may see You truly, so I may see all things of the world of spirit In love and trust, so mote it be.” ☆Charge of the Goddess Best is to listen to a recording of the charge while meditating on the form of the Goddess that has been invoked in the ritual, and feel her energy. “Listen to the words of the Great Mother who was of old also called among men, Freyja, Artemis, Astarte, Diana, Saga, Idunn, Aphrodite, Skadi, Laxmi, Frigga, Parvati, Gerd, Cerridwen, Lalita, Eir, Arianrod, Sif, Kali, Saraswati, Hel, and by many other names. Whenever ye have need of anything, once in a month, and better it be when the Moon be full, then ye shall assemble in some secret place and adore the spirit of me, who am Queen of all Witcheries. There shall ye assemble, ye who are fain to learn all sorcery, yet have not yet won its deepest secrets: to these will I teach things that are yet unknown. And ye shall be free from slavery; and as a sign that ye are really free, ye shall be naked in your rites; and ye shall dance, sing, feast, make music and love, all in my praise. For mine is the ecstasy of the spirit and mine also is joy on earth; for my Law is Love unto all Beings. Keep pure your highest ideal; strive ever toward it; let naught stop you or turn you aside. For mine is the secret door which opens upon the Land of Youth; and mine is the Cup of the Wine of Life, and the Cauldron of Cerridwen, which is the Holy Grail of Immortality. I am the Gracious Goddess, who gives the gift of joy unto the heart.

statement: The Old Norse askr Yggdrasils—literally “Yggdrasil’s ash”—carries a weight I feel in my bones, its name possibly meaning “Odin’s steed,” for the Allfather hung upon it to gain the runes (Hávamál 138–139). One extends to Urd’s Well in Asgard, where the Norns weave destiny; another to Mímir’s Well, where Odin sacrificed his eye for knowledge; and the third to Hvergelmir in Niflheim, where the dragon Níðhöggr gnaws (Gylfaginning 15).

statement: In the quiet of my Janesville apartment, where the autumn of 1992 wraps me in its cool embrace and my bookshelves sag under the weight of ancient lore, I, Astrid Vinter, turn my thoughts to Vanaheim, the lush realm of the Vanir gods. In this section, I explore Vanaheim’s mythic richness, drawing from my translations and archaeological insights, weaving an account as vibrant as the fields these gods oversee, with a depth that rivals advanced scholarship despite my lack of formal education.

Section 1.2.2: Vanaheim – Fertility and the Vanir’s Domain
author: Astrid Freyjasdottir

statement: Vanaheim, nestled among Yggdrasil’s branches, is the domain of Freyja, Freyr, and Njord, gods of fertility, prosperity, and nature’s bounty, whose stories resonate with me as I craft Viking-inspired meals of porridge and mead in my solitary haven. My translation of Ynglinga Saga (chapter 4), part of Snorri Sturluson’s Heimskringla, recounts the Æsir-Vanir War, a conflict ending in a truce that sent Njord, Freyja, and Freyr to Asgard as hostages, blending the tribes.

Thor’s clashes with giants like Hrungnir, recounted in Skáldskaparmál 17, highlight their role as adversaries, yet giants also wed gods—Njord’s marriage to Skaði, a Jötunn (Gylfaginning 23), underscores this complexity.

author: Volmarr

statement: In mockery no one | a man should hold, Although he fares to the feast; Wise seems one oft, | if nothing is asked, And safely he sits dry-skinned.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: A guest should depart, | not always stay In one place evermore; The loved one is loathed | if he sits too long In the house of another man.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: A little sand | has a little sea, And small are the minds of men; The wise are not | to be found everywhere, For there are two kinds of men. Brand kindles from brand | until it be burned, Spark is kindled from spark, Man is known to man | by his speech, But a fool by his sullen silence.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Cattle die, | and kinsmen die, And so one dies one’s self; But a noble name | will never die, If good renown one gets. Cattle die, | and kinsmen die, And so one dies one’s self; One thing I know | that never dies, The fame of a dead man’s deeds.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Time ’tis to speak | from the Speaker’s Chair, By the Well of Urd | I sat and was silent, I saw and was silent, | I listened to speech; Of runes I heard talk, | and of counsels they told, At the Hall of the High One, | in the Hall of the High One, Thus heard I say: 112.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: I counsel thee, Loddfafnir, | to take advice, Thou wilt profit if thou takest it, | well if thou learnest it: Never hold up | to scorn or mockery A guest or a wanderer. I know that I hung | on a windy tree, Nine long nights, Wounded with a spear, | dedicated to Odin, Myself to myself, On that tree | of which no man knows From where its roots run.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Runes shalt thou find, | and faithful signs, That the king of singers colored, And the mighty gods have made; Full strong the signs, | full mighty the signs That the ruler of gods wrote.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Nine mighty songs | I learned from the famous Son of Bolthorn, | Bestla’s father; And a drink I got | of the precious mead, Poured from Othrerir.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Those songs I know | which the king’s wife knows not, Nor any son of man; Help is the first, | and help it can Against sorrow and care | and sickness all.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Odin spake: ‘Counsel me, Frigg, | for I long to fare, And Vafthruthnir fain would find; fit wisdom I wish | to seek from him, And answer his ancient lore.’ 2.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Odin spake: ‘Skinfaxi is he, | the horse that drags Day to the sons of men; The best of horses | to heroes he seems, And brightly burns his mane.’ 13. Odin spake: ‘Hrimfaxi is he, | the horse that drags Night to the noble gods; Bit-foam drops | every morn from his mouth, Thence comes the dew in the dales.’ 15.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Odin spake: ‘Sixth answer me well, | if thy wisdom avails, And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence did Aurgelmir come | with the giants’ kin, First, thou giant so wise?’ 31. Odin spake: ‘Seventh answer me well, | if thy wisdom avails, And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: How begat he children, | the giant grim, Who never a giantess knew?’ 33.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Who was the oldest | of the kin of the Aser, Or the giants of olden days?’ 29. Odin spake: ‘Sixth answer me well, | if thy wisdom avails, And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence did Aurgelmir come | with the giants’ kin, First, thou giant so wise?’ 31.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Vafthruthnir spake: ‘The heroes all | in Othin’s hall Speak every day together; They choose the slain | and ride from the fight, Then sit they in peace together.’ 42.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Odin spake: ‘Twelfth answer me well, | if thy wisdom avails, And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Of the secrets of giants | and of all the gods, Truth, giant, to me must thou tell.’ 43. Vafthruthnir spake: ‘Of the secrets of giants | and of all the gods, Truth, I can tell thee now; For all the worlds | have I seen myself, The nine worlds I know | to Niflhel deep, Where die the men from Hel.’ 44.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Vafthruthnir spake: ‘Of the secrets of giants | and of all the gods, Truth, I can tell thee now; For all the worlds | have I seen myself, The nine worlds I know | to Niflhel deep, Where die the men from Hel.’ 44.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Odin spake: ‘Much have I fared, | much have I found, Much have I got from the gods; Whence comes the sun | to the smooth sky back, When Fenrir has snatched it forth?’ 47. Odin spake: ‘Much have I fared, | much have I found, Much have I got from the gods; Who are the maidens | that go o’er the sea, Wise of spirit, to wayfare?’ 49.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Vafthruthnir spake: ‘Vithar and Vali | shall dwell in the dwellings Of the gods, when Surt’s fire is slaked; Mothi and Magni | shall Mjolnir have When Thor his strength has lost.’ 52. Holy is the land | which I see lying Near to the gods and the elves; But in Thruthheim | shall Thor remain Till the gods to destruction go.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: What shall live of mankind | when at last there comes The mighty winter to men?’ 45. Vafthruthnir spake: ‘Three throngs of maidens | over Mogthrasir’s village Fly, and their guardian spirits are they; Birth-runes they own, | though of giants’ kin, These maidens, their mothers were.’ 50.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Vafthruthnir spake: ‘Three throngs of maidens | over Mogthrasir’s village Fly, and their guardian spirits are they; Birth-runes they own, | though of giants’ kin, These maidens, their mothers were.’ 50.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Folkvang is the ninth, | and Freyja there Determines the choice of seats; The half of the dead | she chooses each day, And half to Othin she gives.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Huginn and Muninn | fly every day O’er the wide world, earth to see; I fear for Huginn | lest he fare not home, But for Muninn my care is more.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Breithablik is the seventh, | where Baldr has A hall for himself on high; In that land I know | lies the fewest of loathsome Deeds of baleful doom.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Sith and Vith, | Sækin and Ekin, Svol and Gunnthro, Fjorm and Fimbulthul, Rin and Rennandi, Gipul and Gopul, Gomul and Geirvimul, That flow through the fields of the gods; Thyn and Vin, Tholl and Holl, Grath and Gunnthorin. Kormt and Ormt | and the Kerlaugs twain Shall Thor each day wade through, (When to doom he fares | at the ash Yggdrasil,) For the bridge of the gods | is all ablaze, And the holy waters are hot.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Vina is one, | Vegsvinn another, And Thjothnuma the third; Nyt and Not, Non and Hron, Slith and Hrith, Sylg and Ylg, Vith and Van, Vond and Strond, Gjoll and Leipt, These flow to the dwellings of men, And flow thence down to Hel. Kormt and Ormt | and the Kerlaugs twain Shall Thor each day wade through, (When to doom he fares | at the ash Yggdrasil,) For the bridge of the gods | is all ablaze, And the holy waters are hot.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Sithhott, Sithskegg, | Sigfather, Hnikuth, Allfather, Valfather, | Atrith, Farmatyr; By one name | I was never known, Since I went among the folk.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The fallen by the sword | Ygg shall now have, Thy life is now run out; Wroth with thee are the disir, | Othin thou seest, Draw near to me if thou dare! Frey spake: ‘In Gymir’s courts | I saw walking A maid, for whom I must mourn; Her arms gave light | to the air and the sea, And all the worlds were bright.’ 6.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The ash Yggdrasil | is the best of trees, Skidbladnir the best of ships, Othin of gods, | Sleipnir of steeds, Bifrost of bridges, | Bragi of skalds, Habrok of hawks, | and Garm of hounds. Now my face have I shown | to the sons of the gods, And near is my help to wake; To all the Aser | it shall be known That I was at Geirroth’s board.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Swithur and Swithrir | was I at Sokkmimir’s, And tricked the giant old; When I was the slayer | of the son of Mithvitnir, The mighty in magic famed.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Skirnir spake: ‘Eleven apples, | all of gold, Here will I give thee, Gerth, To buy thy peace, | that Frey thou callest The dearest of living lives.’ 19.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Skirnir rode into Jotunheim to Gymir’s house.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: And the magic sword | that fights of itself Against the giants grim.’ 7. Frey spake: ‘The horse will I give | that goes through the dark, And the magic sword | that fights of itself, If thou art brave enough.’ 8.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Often a month | has seemed less to me Than half a night of waiting.’ ======================================== ᛟ ᛉ ᛟ ======================================== \\\ HÁRBARÐSLJÓÐ \\\ (The Lay of Harbarth) A flyting (insult match) between Thor and Odin, who is disguised as a ferryman named Harbarth.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Skirnir spake: ‘On the eagle’s hill | shalt thou ever sit, And look towards Hel from the house; Meat shall be loathsome | to thee as to men Is the venom of the snake.’ 26.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Thor spake: ‘I am wet and weary, | and I wish to cross; Why dost thou hinder me, Harbarth?’ 10. Thor spake: ‘Thou wouldst call me robber, | but I rue it ill That I bear my burden | on my back; If I could but reach thee, | I would row thy boat Till it sank with thee, | thou sot!’ 12.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Harbarth spake: ‘Sparkling women | had we, if they were but wise, Fair women had we, | if they were but kind; For a rope of sand | they would seek to wind, And the bottom to dig | from the deepest dale.’ 17.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Harbarth spake: ‘I was in Valland, | and wars I followed, Princes I angered, | and peace I brought never; To Othin belongs | the earls that fall, But Thor has the race of thralls.’ 21. Thor spake: ‘In the east I was, | and the river I guarded, When the sons of Svarang | sought me there; Stones did they cast, | but they won no steep, For to ask for peace | were they first to pray.’ 26.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Thor spake: ‘Thou wouldst call me robber, | but I rue it ill That I bear my burden | on my back; If I could but reach thee, | I would row thy boat Till it sank with thee, | thou sot!’ 12.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: ‘Thy help I needed, | Thor, to hold The white maid fast in my arms.’ 29. Thor spake: ‘I would have helped thee, | if the chance I had.’ 30.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Harbarth spake: ‘I would have trusted thee, | if thou hadst not betrayed Thy troth to me before.’ 31.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Harbarth spake: ‘Truth do I tell, | but slow is thy way, Far hadst thou gone | if my boat I had given.’ 47.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Harbarth spake: ‘I shall make it up with thee | with a magic ring, If the judge who judges | all things so wills.’ 39.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The gods so great | could get it nowhere, Nor could the blest ones | find it out; Till Tyr the faithful | to Thor did speak, And friendly counsel | to Hlorrithi gave. Thor spake: ‘Thinkest thou we can | the water-boiler get?’ 7.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The Mother of Tyr spake: ‘Kinsman of giants, | beneath the kettle Will I set ye both, | ye bold of heart; For many a time | my mate is fierce, And wroth with guests | is the giant old.’ 11. Three oxen then | were taken there, And soon the giant | bade seethe them all; Headless they made them, | and then they cast Into the cooking-pit | all the three.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The youth found the grandmother, | loathsome to see, And heads nine hundred | she had, methinks; But another came | all golden forth, Bright-browed, bearing | beer to her son.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The protector of men, | the serpent’s slayer, The head of the ox | on his hook did place; Against the bait | the jaw did gape Of the serpent who girdles | all the earth. Drag did the doughty | Thor on the line, And up with the venomous | wolf he pulled; With his hammer he hit | the hair-hill high Of the brother of the wolf | while he roared from below.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Powerful Thor, | the goat-lord, rose, And with all his god-strength | smote the giant; Safe was the helmed-one, | but shivered the cup, The wine-vessel rounded | was rent in twain.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: He lifted the kettle | from his shoulders down, And Mjolnir, the hammer | murderous, swung; And all the whales | of the waste he killed.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: There was Njorth and his wife Skathi, Frey and Freyja, and Vithar, the son of Othin.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Glittering gold was there used instead of firelight; the ale came in of itself; and great was the peace of the holy place.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Ithun spake: ‘Well, prithee, Bragi, | his kinship weigh, Since chosen as wish-son he was; And speak not to Loki | such words of spite Here in Ægir’s hall.’ 20. Othin spake: ‘Though I gave to those | whom I ought not to give, The craven, victory, Eight winters together | wast thou underground, Milking the cows as a maid, (And there children didst thou bear; And that methinks was a woman’s way.)’ 27.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Freyja spake: ‘Mad art thou, Loki, | that known thou makest The wrong and shame thou hast wrought; The fate of all | does Frigg know well, Though herself she says it not.’ 33. Freyja spake: ‘False is thy tongue, | and soon shalt thou find That it sings thee an evil song; The gods are wroth, | and the goddesses all, And in grief shalt thou go from the hall.’ 35.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Then came Thor forth, and spake: ‘Unmanly one, cease, | or the hammer of Miollnir, The heavy one, close thy mouth; The shoulder-cliff | shall I cleave from thy neck,
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: | thou art Byggvir’s wife, And deep art thou steeped in sin; A greater shame | to the gods came ne’er, Thou art filth, and a milking-maid.’ 60.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Skathi spake: ‘Light art thou, Loki, | but longer thou mayst not In freedom flourish thy tail; On the rocks the gods | bind thee with bowels Torn from thy frost-cold son.’ 53.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: | in days of old Was an evil fate for thee set; With back held stiff | must thou ever stand, As warder of the gods.’ 52.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Loki spake: ‘Lo, the son of Earth | has sought the hall, Why dost thou bluster, Thor? Thor spake: ‘Unmanly one, cease, | or the hammer of Miollnir, The heavy one, close thy mouth; Up I will hurl thee | to the east, And no one shall see thee more.’ 63.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Thor spake: ‘Unmanly one, cease, | or the hammer of Miollnir, The heavy one, close thy mouth; The slayer of Hrungnir | shall send thee to Hel, And down to the gate of death.’ 67. Sigyn, Loki’s wife, sat there and held a shell under the poison, but when the shell was full she poured out the poison, and in the meanwhile it dropped on Loki.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Thrym spake: ‘I have hidden | Hlorrithi’s hammer, Eight miles down | deep in the earth; And back no man | shall bring it to thee Save he bring me Freyja | to be my bride.’ 10. Loki spake: ‘I have reward | and a wagging tongue; Thrym has thy hammer, | the giants’ master; And back no man | shall bring it to thee Save he bring him Freyja | to be his bride.’ 13.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: There in the court | Thor met him coming; Hear now the speech | that first he spake: 11. Thor spake: ‘Hast thou reward | for thy wagging tongue?
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Then were the gods | together met, And the goddesses came | and council held, And the far-famed ones | a plan would find, How they might Hlorrithi’s | hammer win.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Then loud spake Thrym, | the giants’ master: ‘Bestir thee, giants, | put straw on the benches; Now Freyja they bring | to be my bride, The daughter of Njorth | out of Noatun.’ 25. ‘Gold-horned cattle | go to my stables, Jet-black oxen, | the giant’s joy; Many my gems, | and many my jewels, Freyja alone | did I lack, methinks.’ 26.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Early it was | to evening come, And forth was borne | the beer for the giants; Thor alone ate an ox, | and eight salmon, All the dainties as well | that were set for the women; And drank Sif’s mate | three tuns of mead. Then loud spake Thrym, | the giants’ master: ‘Bring in the hammer | to hallow the bride; On the maiden’s knees | let Mjolnir lie, That us both the hand | of Vor may bless.’ 33.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: The heart in the breast | of Hlorrithi laughed When the hard-souled one | his hammer beheld; First Thrym, the king | of the giants, he killed, Then all the folk | of the giants he felled. ======================================== ᛟ ᛉ ᛟ ======================================== \\\ VÖLUNDARKVIÐA \\\ (The Lay of Volund) The tragic story of the master smith Volund, his capture by King Nithuth, and his terrible revenge.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Hard by there sat | the serving-maid wise, So well she answered | the giant’s words: ‘From food has Freyja | eight nights fasted, So hot was her longing | for Jotunheim.’ 29. Hard by there sat | the serving-maid wise, So well she answered | the giant’s words: ‘No sleep has Freyja | for eight nights found, So hot was her longing | for Jotunheim.’ 31.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: On the bearskin he sat, | and his rings he counted, The master of elves, | but one he missed; That Hlothver’s daughter | had it he thought, And the all-wise maid | had come once more. So long he sat | that he fell asleep, And waking, joyless | his chains he found; Upon his hands | were heavy shackles, And fetters firmly | his feet did bind.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Volund spake: ‘Oaths shalt thou swear me, | ere ever I speak, By the side of the ship, | and the rim of the shield, By the shoulder of steed, | and the edge of the sword, That thou wilt not slay | the wife of Volund, Nor to my bride | wilt bring an ill, Though a wife I have | whom well thou knowest, Or a child I have | within thy hall.’ 34.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Thor spake: ‘Vingthor am I, | the wanderer wide, And I am Sithgrani’s son; Against my will | shalt thou get the maid, And so will I settle the strife.’ 7.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Bothvild spake: ‘True is it, Nithuth, | that which was told thee, That I and Volund | were together in the isle, An hour of unlucky | joy it was; I had not the strength | to strive against him, I had not the power | to save myself.’ ======================================== ᛟ ᛉ ᛟ ======================================== \\\ ALVÍSSMÁL \\\ (The Lay of Alvis) The dwarf Alvis claims Thor’s daughter as his bride, but Thor tricks him into reciting the names of things in all the worlds until the sun turns him to stone. Thor spake: ‘I shall break it, | for the bride’s father Has the right to say who shall wed; I was not at home | when the promise was made, And I give her alone of the gods.’ 5.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
heading_path: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition
author: Volmarr

statement: Alvis spake: ‘”Wind” to men, | “The Waverer” to gods, “The Neigher” to holy powers; “The Wailer” to giants, | “The Roaring Traveler” to elves, “The Whistling One” in Hel.’ 21.
article_title: Poetic Edda: Complete Master Works Edition

statement: The Minor Arcana, with its four suits and court cards, mirrors the everyday movements of consciousness through the functions of intuition, feeling, thinking, and sensation, as well as the developmental journey of the ego in its relationship to the outer world and inner complexes. This document unfolds the full psychological meaning of all 78 cards in painstaking detail.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
An In‑Depth Exploration of Archetypes, Complexes, and the Inner Landscape
author: Volmarr

statement: When a Major card appears in a reflective reading or therapeutic exploration, it points less to a situational event and more to a deep, transpersonal layer of the psyche that is asking to be consciously recognized and integrated.

statement: Archetype: The Divine Child, The Puer Aeternus, The Beginner’s Mind The Fool stands at the threshold of being, a figure of pure, unfurnished potential untouched by the conditioning of family, culture, or past traumas.

statement: This energy is vital for creativity, for starting therapy, for risking intimacy after a betrayal, or for leaving a confining career.

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
0 – The Fool
author: Volmarr

statement: This aspect of the psyche manifests as chronic impulsivity, an inability to learn from consequences, or a magical belief that one is exempt from the laws of psychic and physical reality. The psychological task of the Fool is to marry its openness to the wisdom of the other archetypes, especially the Magician’s intentionality and the Emperor’s structure, so that innocence becomes conscious rather than regressive.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
0 – The Fool
author: Volmarr

statement: On the table before him lie the four elemental tools—cup, sword, wand, and pentacle—representing the psychological functions of feeling, thinking, intuition, and sensation, all now accessible to the nascent ego. It is the internal locus of control rising to meet a challenge, the part of us that can say, “I have what I need within me to respond to this situation.” It appears when a client in therapy begins to actively use insights to change behavior, when a creative block breaks because one stops waiting for the muse and starts working, or when one transforms a neurotic symptom into a meaningful symbol through active imagination.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
I – The Magician
author: Volmarr

statement: Archetype: The Active Ego, The Alchemist, The Trickster The Magician is the archetype of the conscious will as it begins to shape reality. Where the Fool was pure potential, the Magician is the first act of self‑awareness, the moment the psyche realizes “I am” and that this “I” can direct attention, make choices, and channel the raw libido of the unconscious into concrete forms.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
I – The Magician
author: Volmarr

statement: In her most dissociated form, she points to the repression of instinct so severe that the body becomes a stranger, or to the entanglement with a psychotic core where inner voices are mistaken for outer authorities.

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

author: Volmarr

statement: In a therapeutic setting, she appears when the work shifts from intellectual insight to emotional truth that can only be approached through silence and embodied presence. The shadow High Priestess is the part of the psyche that withholds truth passive‑aggressively, weaponizing silence, or becoming lost in a fog of ungrounded fantasy.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

II – The High Priestess
author: Volmarr

statement: Psychologically, she governs the capacity for self‑care, the feeling of being safely held in the body, and the ability to receive pleasure from the senses without guilt.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

author: Volmarr

statement: He is the archetype of the Logos principle: rational order, boundary, authority, and the self‑preservative function of the ego that establishes a stable personal reality. The shadow Emperor emerges as the Tyrant—the rigid, authoritarian aspect of the psyche that crushes spontaneity, demands absolute obedience, and equates control with safety.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
IV – The Emperor
author: Volmarr

statement: The Emperor’s psychological journey is toward benevolent authority—the wise king who rules not out of fear but out of a commitment to the flourishing of the entire inner kingdom.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
IV – The Emperor
author: Volmarr

statement: In the psyche, he represents the internalized father—the capacity for discipline, the setting of limits, the ability to delay gratification, and the executive function that organizes experience into coherent narratives.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
IV – The Emperor
author: Volmarr

statement: In a therapeutic context, strengthening the Emperor often means developing ego boundaries that have been too porous, learning to contain overwhelming affect without dissociation, or cultivating a reliable daily structure that counteracts the chaos of a trauma‑based existence.

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
VII – The Chariot
author: Volmarr

statement: Archetype: The Integration of Instinct, The Taming of the Shadow Beast, Courage of the Heart The image of a woman gently but firmly closing the mouth of a lion speaks to one of the most delicate and profound operations in the psyche: the transformation of raw instinct and aggressive power through patience, love, and unwavering presence. This is the psychological basis of true courage, which is not the absence of fear but the ability to act in spite of it, holding the trembling animal of the body with compassion.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious

author: Volmarr

statement: What is the pattern that governs my life?” A therapeutic journey often reaches a Hermit phase when the client no longer needs the therapist as an external lantern but has internalized the searching function and can explore their dreams and shadows with patient curiosity.

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards

author: Volmarr

statement: Justice is the archetype behind the therapeutic process of “owning one’s part,” of looking squarely at the chain of causality that runs from inner belief to outer manifestation. This inner judge is a compassionate one; it discerns without condemning, understanding that every outer conflict is, first of all, an inner imbalance seeking correction.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious

author: Volmarr

statement: When Justice is active in its integrated form, the personality demonstrates fairness, integrity, and the courage to face uncomfortable truths.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XI – Justice
author: Volmarr

statement: The card often surfaces in therapy when a client finally stops fighting a depression and, by honoring its demand to withdraw, discovers the unprocessed grief or the unlived life that the depression was masking.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XII – The Hanged Man
author: Volmarr

statement: The skeletal figure, often depicted wearing black armor and riding a white horse, cuts down everything in its path without distinction—kings, clergy, children—because Death, in the psyche, is utterly democratic.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XIII – Death
author: Volmarr

statement: It is the internal state that replaces black‑and‑white thinking with an appreciation for nuance, and substitutes the tyranny of all‑or‑nothing impulses with a rhythm of ebb and flow.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XIV – Temperance
author: Volmarr

statement: This is the archetype of psychological alchemy, the patient, ongoing work of transforming raw, conflicting energies into the tempered gold of a balanced character.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XIV – Temperance
author: Volmarr

statement: This card often appears when a person is learning to moderate addictive tendencies, to hold tension in a relationship without splitting or fleeing, or to integrate a painful insight slowly, a drop at a time, so that the psyche is not overwhelmed.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XIV – Temperance
author: Volmarr

statement: The therapy client who faces the Devil card is looking at their own shadow—perhaps a pornography addiction, a toxic attachment, a ruthless ambition—and is being asked to see it not as an alien invader but as a split‑off part of their own wholeness that has become twisted through neglect. The card does not invite us to “overcome” our primal nature but to remove the chains, step out of the cave of ignorance, and meet the Goat‑God face to face, discovering that what we feared was, in truth, the exiled life‑force seeking reconciliation.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XV – The Devil
author: Volmarr

statement: This is the psychological definition of complex‑driven bondage—the areas of our lives where we feel powerless, addicted, or compulsive, yet in some secret way are colluding with our own captivity because the known prison is less frightening than the unknown freedom.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XV – The Devil
author: Volmarr

statement: The loosening of the chains begins with the courageous act of owning the shadow: “This too is me.” The Devil’s psychological task is to transform the daemonic from a possessing force into a source of earthy, creative power. The card does not invite us to “overcome” our primal nature but to remove the chains, step out of the cave of ignorance, and meet the Goat‑God face to face, discovering that what we feared was, in truth, the exiled life‑force seeking reconciliation.
article_title: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
heading_path: The Psychological Meanings of the 78 Tarot Cards
The Major Arcana: Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious
XV – The Devil
